newsitem.title: UK: Strong performance prompts Hungary stock slide.
newsitem.headline: Strong performance prompts Hungary stock slide.

text.p: Recent mixed earnings from Hungarian companies have not inspired foreign investors to take profits, rather the 2,000 point gain in the bourse this year to over 3,500 points has meant some are locking in gains.
"Although third-quarter results may have been patchy, I do not think they have been so bad that people would leave the market," said Nathan West, an equities salesman at Daiwa Europe in London.
Companies in the A category of the Budapest Stock Exchange have just finished releasing their January-September results.

On November 12, shares in leading pharmaceuticals maker Egis plunged 500 forints to 8,500 after it reported a rise in after-tax profit to 4.1 billion forints ($26 million) from 3.8 billion a year ago, less than many analysts had expected.
In a note to investors CSFB cut its outlook for full year earnings, but said that the fall in the company's share price leads it to see the stock as representing value for investors.
The stock finished at 8,000 forints on Tuesday, up 100 from Monday's close.
"The earnings reports have been a mixed bag," said Tom Chadwick, vice president of Merrill Lynch emerging markets in London.
Another pharmaceutical stock, Richter, reported a rise in after-tax profit to nine billion forints in January to September from 6.3 billion a year earlier.
"There was a perception that Egis' results were not quite good as expected...while Richter's results were generally perceived here as good," Daiwa's West said.
Earnings from the Hungarian market's largest capitalisation stock, oil and gas giant MOL on November 14 divided opinion.
Its after-tax group earnings surged to 11 billion forints from 2.1 billion.
"There was no surprise at MOL. The results at the moment are less relevant than prospective price rises in the Hungarian energy market," West said.
The Hungarian government is set to announce the terms of a rise in oil and gas prices on Thursday and expectations are for a rise of 20-25 percent.

Merrill's Chadwick is bullish on MOL after its earnings and has upgraded the stock to "accumulate" from "neutral". "MOL did far better than expected," he said, attributing the oil company's results to higher world oil prices.
While the current depression of the consumer market in Hungary is likely to weigh on this year's earnings, western investors are bullish on the outlook for the export sector.
"At the moment it's the export-led companies which are still doing better," West said. "The Hungarian market is incredibly difficult to operate in."
Nevertheless, there are some who believe the outlook for the domestic market is rosier than it has been for some time.
Budapest Bank, a Hungarian bank unit of General Electric Capital Corp of the U.S. expects an economic upturn in 1997 to be based on internal factors.

Budapest Bank said it expected Hungary's economic growth to pick up to one to three percent in 1997 from zero to half a percent this year on the back of domestic expansion and a recovery in consumption.

Western investors also remain sanguine on the outlook for the Budapest bourse, which has been one of the top performers of 1996, but note that the market will have to wait for further gains until 1997.
"The bourse will remain flat or move slightly down until the end of the year but I'm very positive of the market for next year," said Daiwa's West.
However, he did not hide his opinion that the Budapest bourse will have to face more competition from other markets in the region after this year's strong performance. ($1=159.10 Forint)
